claim: Thalidomide was first marketed in the 1950s as a nonaddictive, nonbarbiturate sedative with anti-emetic properties.
source: Thalidomide was first marketed in the 1950s as a nonaddictive, nonbarbiturate sedative with anti-emetic properties, and was widely used to treat morning sickness in pregnant women.
evidence: This is a historical fact stated in the introduction without experimental data from this study.

claim: Thalidomide was widely used to treat morning sickness in pregnant women.
source: Thalidomide was first marketed in the 1950s as a nonaddictive, nonbarbiturate sedative with anti-emetic properties, and was widely used to treat morning sickness in pregnant women.
evidence: This is a historical fact stated in the introduction.

claim: In 1961, two independent reports confirmed that thalidomide was causative to the largest preventable medical disaster in modern history.
source: In 1961, two independent reports confirmed that thalidomide was causative to this, the largest preventable medical disaster in modern history (Lenz, 1962; McBride, 1961).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical reports.

claim: Thousands of children were born with severe birth defects due to thalidomide.
source: In addition to thousands of children born with severe birth defects, there were reports of increased miscarriage rates during this period (Lenz, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a historical report.

claim: There were reports of increased miscarriage rates during the thalidomide period.
source: In addition to thousands of children born with severe birth defects, there were reports of increased miscarriage rates during this period (Lenz, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a historical report.

claim: Thalidomide and its close derivatives, lenalidomide and pomalidomide, are known as immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs).
source: Despite this tragedy, thalidomide, and its close derivatives, lenalidomide and pomalidomide, known as immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs), continue to be used to treat a variety of clinical conditions such as multiple myeloma (MM) and 5q-deletion associated myelodysplastic syndrome (del(5q)-MDS) (D'Amato et al., 1994; Pan and Lentzsch, 2012).
evidence: This is established nomenclature supported by citations.

claim: IMiDs continue to be used to treat multiple myeloma (MM) and 5q-deletion associated myelodysplastic syndrome (del(5q)-MDS).
source: Despite this tragedy, thalidomide, and its close derivatives, lenalidomide and pomalidomide, known as immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs), continue to be used to treat a variety of clinical conditions such as multiple myeloma (MM) and 5q-deletion associated myelodysplastic syndrome (del(5q)-MDS) (D'Amato et al., 1994; Pan and Lentzsch, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Thalidomide and analogs exert their therapeutic effect by binding to the Cullin RING E3 ubiquitin ligase CUL4-RBX1-DDB1-CRBN (CRL4CRBN).
source: It was only recently shown that thalidomide and analogs exert their therapeutic effect by binding to the Cullin RING E3 ubiquitin ligase CUL4-RBX1-DDB1-CRBN (CRL4CRBN) (Chamberlain et al., 2014; Fischer et al., 2014; Ito et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: IMiDs promote ubiquitination and degradation of the zinc finger transcription factors IKAROS (IKZF1), AIOLOS (IKZF3), and ZFP91.
source: It was only recently shown that thalidomide and analogs exert their therapeutic effect by binding to the Cullin RING E3 ubiquitin ligase CUL4-RBX1-DDB1-CRBN (CRL4CRBN) (Chamberlain et al., 2014; Fischer et al., 2014; Ito et al., 2010) and promoting ubiquitination and degradation of key efficacy targets (neo-substrates), such as the zinc finger (ZnF) transcription factors IKAROS (IKZF1), AIOLOS (IKZF3), and ZFP91 (An et al., 2017; Fischer et al., 2014; Gandhi et al., 2014b; Krönke et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: IMiDs can promote degradation of targets that lack a zinc finger domain, including Casein Kinase 1 alpha (CSNK1A1) and GSPT1.
source: IMiDs can also promote degradation of targets that lack a zinc finger domain, including Casein Kinase 1 alpha (CSNK1A1) (Krönke et al., 2015; Petzold et al., 2016) and GSPT1 (Matyskiela et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CRL4CRBN has been implicated in the IMiD-independent turnover of GLUL, BSG, and MEIS2.
source: CRL4CRBN has further been implicated in the IMiD-independent turnover of GLUL, BSG, and MEIS2 (Eichner et al., 2016; Krönke et al., 2014; Nguyen et al., 2016;Fischer et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CRL4CRBN has been implicated in regulation of AMPK.
source: CRL4CRBN has further been implicated in the IMiD-independent turnover of GLUL, BSG, and MEIS2 (Eichner et al., 2016; Krönke et al., 2014; Nguyen et al., 2016;Fischer et al., 2014), and regulation of AMPK (Lee et al., 2013), processes potentially inhibited by IMiDs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: All known IMiD-dependent CRL4CRBN substrates share the characteristic β-hairpin loop structure.
source: Although no obvious sequence homology exists between the known IMiD-dependent CRL4CRBN substrates, all share the characteristic β-hairpin loop structure observed in X-ray crystal structures of IMiDs bound to CRBN and CSNK1A1 or GSPT1 (Matyskiela et al., 2016; Petzold et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: All known IMiD-dependent CRL4CRBN substrates share a key glycine residue that engages the phthalimide moiety of IMiDs.
source: Although no obvious sequence homology exists between the known IMiD-dependent CRL4CRBN substrates, all share the characteristic β-hairpin loop structure observed in X-ray crystal structures of IMiDs bound to CRBN and CSNK1A1 or GSPT1 (Matyskiela et al., 2016; Petzold et al., 2016), and a key glycine residue that engages the phthalimide moiety of IMiDs (An et al., 2017; Matyskiela et al., 2016; Petzold et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Species such as mice, rats, and bush babies are resistant to thalidomide-induced teratogenicity.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that species such as mice, rats, and bush babies are resistant to thalidomide-induced teratogenicity (Butler, 1977; Heger et al., 1988; Ingalls et al., 1964; Vickers, 1967)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SALL4 showed statistically significant downregulation across all three IMiD treatments (thalidomide, lenalidomide, pomalidomide) in H9 hESC with a change in protein abundance greater than 1.5-fold and p value < 0.001.
source: From ~10,000 proteins quantified in H9 hESC, only the developmental spalt-like transcription factor SALL4 showed statistically significant downregulation across all three drug treatments with a change in protein abundance greater than 1.5-fold, and a p value < 0.001 (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Treatment with lenalidomide led to degradation of CSNK1A1.
source: In accordance with previous findings, we also observed that treatment with lenalidomide led to degradation of CSNK1A1 (Krönke et al., 2015; Petzold et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous findings and is consistent with the current study's observations.

claim: Pomalidomide induced degradation of ZFP91, ZBTB39, FAM83F, WIZ, RAB28, and DTWD1.
source: Pomalidomide induced degradation of additional targets, including the previously characterized zinc finger protein ZFP91 (An et al., 2017) and the largely uncharacterized proteins ZBTB39, FAM83F, WIZ, RAB28, and DTWD1 (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Comprehensive proteomics studies revealed multiple novel substrates for IMiDs: ZNF692, SALL4, RNF166, FAM83F, ZNF827, RAB28, ZBTB39, ZNF653, DTWD1, ZNF98, and GZF1.
source: Comprehensive proteomics studies across multiple independent replicates of hESC, Kelly, SK-N-DZ, and MM1s cells (Figure 1A–D, see Materials and methods and Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2 for details), revealed multiple novel substrates for IMiDs (ZNF692, SALL4, RNF166, FAM83F, ZNF827, RAB28, ZBTB39, ZNF653, DTWD1, ZNF98, and GZF1).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data across multiple cell lines.

claim: Inhibition of the Cullin RING ligase (CRL) by MLN4924 fully abrogated IMiD-induced degradation of targets.
source: Inhibition of the Cullin RING ligase (CRL) by MLN4924 fully abrogated IMiD-induced degradation of targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C), and thereby confirmed the CRL-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by rescue proteomics experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Eight of the 11 new targets found in the proteomics screen are ZnF proteins (SALL4, ZNF827, ZBTB39, RNF166, ZNF653, ZNF692, ZNF98 and GZF1).
source: Eight of the 11 new targets found in the proteomics screen are ZnF proteins (SALL4, ZNF827, ZBTB39, RNF166, ZNF653, ZNF692, ZNF98 and GZF1)
evidence: This is based on analysis of the proteomics data and protein domain information.

claim: All ZnF targets except RNF166 contain at least one ZnF domain that has the characteristic features previously described as critical for IMiD-dependent degradation.
source: Eight of the 11 new targets found in the proteomics screen are ZnF proteins (SALL4, ZNF827, ZBTB39, RNF166, ZNF653, ZNF692, ZNF98 and GZF1), and except for RNF166, all contain at least one ZnF domain that has the characteristic features previously described as critical for IMiD-dependent degradation (An et al., 2017) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and citation to prior work.

claim: Thalidomide induces robust degradation of the zinc finger transcription factors ZNF692, SALL4, and the ubiquitin ligase RNF166 in cell lines expressing detectable levels of those proteins.
source: We find that thalidomide induces robust degradation of the zinc finger transcription factors ZNF692, SALL4, and the ubiquitin ligase RNF166 in cell lines expressing detectable levels of those proteins (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Lenalidomide results in additional degradation of ZNF827, FAM83F, and RAB28 along with the lenalidomide-specific substrate CSNK1A1.
source: Lenalidomide results in additional degradation of ZNF827, FAM83F, and RAB28 along with the lenalidomide-specific substrate CSNK1A1.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data.

claim: Pomalidomide induces robust degradation of ZBTB39, ZFP91, DTWD1, and ZNF653.
source: Pomalidomide shows the most pronounced expansion of targets, and in addition induces robust degradation of ZBTB39, ZFP91, DTWD1, and ZNF653.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data.

claim: DTWD1 is a non zinc finger target that was found to be robustly degraded by pomalidomide.
source: It is interesting to note that DTWD1 is, as CSNK1A1 and GSPT1, another non zinc finger target that was found to be robustly degraded by pomalidomide.
evidence: This is based on proteomics data and comparison with known non-ZnF targets.

claim: Familial loss of function (LOF) mutations in SALL4 are causatively linked to Duane Radial Ray syndrome (DRRS) also known as Okihiro syndrome.
source: Strikingly, human genetic research has shown that familial loss of function (LOF) mutations in SALL4 are causatively linked to the clinical syndromes, Duane Radial Ray syndrome (DRRS) also known as Okihiro syndrome, and mutated in some patients with Holt-Oram syndrome (HOS). Remarkably, both DRRS and HOS have large phenotypic overlaps with thalidomide embryopathy (Kohlhase et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to human genetic research.

claim: SALL4 mutations are found in some patients with Holt-Oram syndrome (HOS).
source: Strikingly, human genetic research has shown that familial loss of function (LOF) mutations in SALL4 are causatively linked to the clinical syndromes, Duane Radial Ray syndrome (DRRS) also known as Okihiro syndrome, and mutated in some patients with Holt-Oram syndrome (HOS). Remarkably, both DRRS and HOS have large phenotypic overlaps with thalidomide embryopathy (Kohlhase et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to human genetic research.

claim: Both DRRS and HOS have large phenotypic overlaps with thalidomide embryopathy.
source: Remarkably, both DRRS and HOS have large phenotypic overlaps with thalidomide embryopathy (Kohlhase et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: The phenotypic resemblance between DRRS/HOS and thalidomide embryopathy has led to misdiagnosis of patients with SALL4 mutations as cases of thalidomide embryopathy.
source: Remarkably, both DRRS and HOS have large phenotypic overlaps with thalidomide embryopathy (Kohlhase et al., 2003), and this phenotypic resemblance has led to misdiagnosis of patients with SALL4 mutations as cases of thalidomide embryopathy and the hypothesis that the tbx5/sall4 axis might be involved in thalidomide pathogenesis (Knobloch and Rüther, 2008; Kohlhase et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: The penetrance of DRRS in individuals with heterozygous SALL4 mutations likely exceeds 90%.
source: The penetrance of DRRS in individuals with heterozygous SALL4 mutations likely exceeds 90% (Kohlhase, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: All currently described SALL4 mutations are heterozygous LOF mutations.
source: All currently described SALL4 mutations are heterozygous LOF mutations, and the absence of homozygous mutations indicates the essentiality of the gene.
evidence: This is based on review of genetic literature.

claim: Homozygous deletion of Sall4 is early embryonic lethal in mice.
source: Accordingly, homozygous deletion of Sall4 is early embryonic lethal in mice (Sakaki-Yumoto et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to mouse genetic studies.

claim: Mice with heterozygous deletion of Sall4 show a high frequency of miscarriage.
source: Mice with heterozygous deletion of Sall4 show a high frequency of miscarriage, while surviving litters show ventricular septal defects and anal stenosis, both phenotypes that are observed in humans with DRRS or thalidomide syndrome (Sakaki-Yumoto et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to mouse genetic studies.

claim: Surviving litters of mice with heterozygous deletion of Sall4 show ventricular septal defects and anal stenosis.
source: Mice with heterozygous deletion of Sall4 show a high frequency of miscarriage, while surviving litters show ventricular septal defects and anal stenosis, both phenotypes that are observed in humans with DRRS or thalidomide syndrome (Sakaki-Yumoto et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to mouse genetic studies.

claim: Mice carrying a heterozygous Sall4 genetrap allele show defects in heart and limb development, partially reminiscent of patients with DRRS or HOS.
source: Mice carrying a heterozygous Sall4 genetrap allele show defects in heart and limb development, partially reminiscent of patients with DRRS or HOS (Koshiba-Takeuchi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to mouse genetic studies.

claim: Roberts syndrome is caused by mutations in the ESCO2 gene.
source: Another genetic disorder with a related phenotype is Roberts syndrome, caused by mutations in the ESCO2 gene (Afifi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to genetic literature.

claim: ESCO2 protein levels were found to be unchanged in all mass spectrometry experiments despite robust and ubiquitous expression.
source: While ESCO2 similarly encodes for a zinc finger protein and is transcriptionally regulated by ZNF143 (Nishihara et al., 2010), ESCO2 (as well as ZNF143, SALL1, SALL2, and SALL3) protein levels were found to be unchanged in all of our mass spectrometry experiments despite robust and ubiquitous expression (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2 and Figure 1—source data 1–14).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: ZNF143, SALL1, SALL2, and SALL3 protein levels were found to be unchanged in all mass spectrometry experiments despite robust and ubiquitous expression.
source: While ESCO2 similarly encodes for a zinc finger protein and is transcriptionally regulated by ZNF143 (Nishihara et al., 2010), ESCO2 (as well as ZNF143, SALL1, SALL2, and SALL3) protein levels were found to be unchanged in all of our mass spectrometry experiments despite robust and ubiquitous expression (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2 and Figure 1—source data 1–14).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: A dose-dependent decrease in SALL4 protein levels was observed with all three IMiD analogs (thalidomide, lenalidomide, pomalidomide) in H9 hESC.
source: To extend our mass spectrometry findings, we treated H9 hESC with increasing doses of thalidomide, lenalidomide, pomalidomide, or with DMSO as a control, and assessed protein levels of SALL4 by western blot. We observed a dose-dependent decrease in protein levels with all three drugs (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Thalidomide treatment does not reduce the level of SALL4 mRNA, but rather upregulates SALL4 mRNA.
source: We then used qPCR to confirm that thalidomide treatment does not reduce the level of SALL4 mRNA, but rather upregulates SALL4 mRNA, consistent with the protein-level changes being caused by post-transcriptional effects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claim: A dose-dependent decrease in SALL4 protein levels was observed with all three IMiD analogs in Kelly, SK-N-DZ, HEK293T, and H661 cells.
source: We next sought to assess the robustness of SALL4 degradation across different lineages by subjecting a panel of cell lines (Kelly, SK-N-DZ, HEK293T, and H661 cells) to increasing concentrations of thalidomide, lenalidomide, pomalidomide, or DMSO as a control and performed western blot analysis (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C). We observed a dose-dependent decrease in SALL4 protein levels with all three IMiD analogs and in all tested cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: IMiD-induced degradation of SALL4 was abrogated by co-treatment with the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib.
source: In accordance with a CRL4CRBN-dependent mechanism, the IMiD-induced degradation was abrogated by co-treatment with the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib, the NEDD8 inhibitor MLN4924, or the ubiquitin E1 (UBA1) inhibitor MLN7243 (which blocks all cellular ubiquitination by inhibiting the initial step of the ubiquitin conjugation cascade) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: IMiD-induced degradation of SALL4 was abrogated by co-treatment with the NEDD8 inhibitor MLN4924.
source: In accordance with a CRL4CRBN-dependent mechanism, the IMiD-induced degradation was abrogated by co-treatment with the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib, the NEDD8 inhibitor MLN4924, or the ubiquitin E1 (UBA1) inhibitor MLN7243 (which blocks all cellular ubiquitination by inhibiting the initial step of the ubiquitin conjugation cascade) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: IMiD-induced degradation of SALL4 was abrogated by co-treatment with the ubiquitin E1 (UBA1) inhibitor MLN7243.
source: In accordance with a CRL4CRBN-dependent mechanism, the IMiD-induced degradation was abrogated by co-treatment with the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib, the NEDD8 inhibitor MLN4924, or the ubiquitin E1 (UBA1) inhibitor MLN7243 (which blocks all cellular ubiquitination by inhibiting the initial step of the ubiquitin conjugation cascade) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: No degradation of SALL4 was observed in CRBN-/- cells upon IMiD treatment.
source: To further evaluate the CRL4CRBN-dependent mechanism, we generated CRBN-/- Kelly and HEK293T cells using CRISPR/Cas9 technology and treated the resulting CRBN-/- cells and parental cells with increasing concentrations of thalidomide, lenalidomide, or pomalidomide (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F). In agreement with the CRBN-dependent mechanism, no degradation of SALL4 was observed in CRBN-/- cells.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Thalidomide has a plasma half-life (t1/2) of ~6 to 8 h.
source: Thalidomide has a plasma half-life (t1/2) of ~6 to 8 h (~3 h for lenalidomide, ~9 h for pomalidomide) and a maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) of ~5–10 µM (~2.5 µM for lenalidomide, 0.05 µM for pomalidomide) upon a typical dose of 200–400 mg, 25 mg, or 2 mg for thalidomide, lenalidomide, or pomalidomide, respectively (Chen et al., 2017; Hoffmann et al., 2013; Teo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to pharmacokinetic studies.

claim: Lenalidomide has a plasma half-life (t1/2) of ~3 h.
source: Thalidomide has a plasma half-life (t1/2) of ~6 to 8 h (~3 h for lenalidomide, ~9 h for pomalidomide) and a maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) of ~5–10 µM (~2.5 µM for lenalidomide, 0.05 µM for pomalidomide) upon a typical dose of 200–400 mg, 25 mg, or 2 mg for thalidomide, lenalidomide, or pomalidomide, respectively (Chen et al., 2017; Hoffmann et al., 2013; Teo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to pharmacokinetic studies.

claim: Pomalidomide has a plasma half-life (t1/2) of ~9 h.
source: Thalidomide has a plasma half-life (t1/2) of ~6 to 8 h (~3 h for lenalidomide, ~9 h for pomalidomide) and a maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) of ~5–10 µM (~2.5 µM for lenalidomide, 0.05 µM for pomalidomide) upon a typical dose of 200–400 mg, 25 mg, or 2 mg for thalidomide, lenalidomide, or pomalidomide, respectively (Chen et al., 2017; Hoffmann et al., 2013; Teo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to pharmacokinetic studies.

claim: Thalidomide has a maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) of ~5–10 µM upon a typical dose of 200–400 mg.
source: Thalidomide has a plasma half-life (t1/2) of ~6 to 8 h (~3 h for lenalidomide, ~9 h for pomalidomide) and a maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) of ~5–10 µM (~2.5 µM for lenalidomide, 0.05 µM for pomalidomide) upon a typical dose of 200–400 mg, 25 mg, or 2 mg for thalidomide, lenalidomide, or pomalidomide, respectively (Chen et al., 2017; Hoffmann et al., 2013; Teo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to pharmacokinetic studies.

claim: Lenalidomide has a maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) of ~2.5 µM upon a typical dose of 25 mg.
source: Thalidomide has a plasma half-life (t1/2) of ~6 to 8 h (~3 h for lenalidomide, ~9 h for pomalidomide) and a maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) of ~5–10 µM (~2.5 µM for lenalidomide, 0.05 µM for pomalidomide) upon a typical dose of 200–400 mg, 25 mg, or 2 mg for thalidomide, lenalidomide, or pomalidomide, respectively (Chen et al., 2017; Hoffmann et al., 2013; Teo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to pharmacokinetic studies.

claim: Pomalidomide has a maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) of ~0.05 µM upon a typical dose of 2 mg.
source: Thalidomide has a plasma half-life (t1/2) of ~6 to 8 h (~3 h for lenalidomide, ~9 h for pomalidomide) and a maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) of ~5–10 µM (~2.5 µM for lenalidomide, 0.05 µM for pomalidomide) upon a typical dose of 200–400 mg, 25 mg, or 2 mg for thalidomide, lenalidomide, or pomalidomide, respectively (Chen et al., 2017; Hoffmann et al., 2013; Teo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to pharmacokinetic studies.

claim: Treatment with pomalidomide induces degradation of SALL4 as early as 4 h post treatment.
source: Treatment with pomalidomide induces degradation of SALL4 as early as 4 h post treatment (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: This is supported by western blot time course data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: SALL4 protein levels recovered to levels close to pre-treatment level after 48 h post washout of pomalidomide.
source: Treatment with pomalidomide induces degradation of SALL4 as early as 4 h post treatment (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H), which recovered to levels close to pre-treatment level after 48 h post washout (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is supported by western blot washout data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A single dose of IMiD drugs will be sufficient to deplete SALL4 protein levels for >24 h.
source: Treatment with pomalidomide induces degradation of SALL4 as early as 4 h post treatment (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H), which recovered to levels close to pre-treatment level after 48 h post washout (Figure 2E), together suggesting that a single dose of IMiD drugs will be sufficient to deplete SALL4 protein levels for >24 h.
evidence: This is inferred from the time course and washout data.

claim: The second (SALL4ZnF2) and fourth (SALL4ZnF4) ZnF domains of SALL4 (aa 410–433, and aa 594–616, respectively) were identified as candidate degrons for IMiD-induced binding.
source: Based on conserved features among IMiD-sensitive ZnF domains (Figure 3A, C–x(2)-C-G motif within the canonical C2H2 zinc finger motif), the second (SALL4ZnF2) and fourth (SALL4ZnF4) ZnF domains of SALL4 (aa 410–433, and aa 594–616, respectively) were identified as candidate degrons for IMiD-induced binding.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Dose-dependent binding was observed between SALL4ZnF2 or SALL4ZnF4 and CRBN similar to that described for IKZF1/3 and ZFP91.
source: We observed dose-dependent binding between SALL4ZnF2 or SALL4ZnF4 and CRBN similar to that described for IKZF1/3 and ZFP91, albeit with reduced apparent affinity for SALL4ZnF4 (Figure 3B,C) (Petzold et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by TR-FRET binding data shown in Figure 3B,C and citation to prior work.

claim: SALL4ZnF4 has reduced apparent affinity for CRBN compared to SALL4ZnF2.
source: We observed dose-dependent binding between SALL4ZnF2 or SALL4ZnF4 and CRBN similar to that described for IKZF1/3 and ZFP91, albeit with reduced apparent affinity for SALL4ZnF4 (Figure 3B,C) (Petzold et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by TR-FRET binding data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: A construct spanning ZnF1 and ZnF2 of SALL4 (SALL4ZnF1-2) exhibited tighter binding to CRBN than SALL4ZnF2 alone.
source: However, we noticed that a construct spanning ZnF1 and ZnF2 of SALL4 (SALL4ZnF1-2) exhibited even tighter binding to CRBN (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B) and enhanced dose-dependent complex formation in TR-FRET (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by TR-FRET binding data shown in Figure 3D, 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Multiple zinc finger domains of SALL4 contribute to binding to CRBN, and may result in multivalent recruitment to CRBN in vivo.
source: These findings suggest that multiple zinc finger domains of SALL4 contribute to binding, and may result in multivalent recruitment to CRBN in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding data showing enhanced affinity with tandem ZnF constructs.

claim: The rank order of Pom >Thal >> Len in binding observed with ZnF2 is in accordance with the cellular potency in degradation of SALL4.
source: However, the strength of the interaction with ZnF4 is unlikely to be sufficient for degradation in cells, and moreover, the rank order of Pom >Thal >> Len in binding observed with ZnF2 is in accordance with the cellular potency in degradation of SALL4, suggesting that ZnF2 is the critical ZnF domain for SALL4 degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing in vitro binding data with cellular degradation data.

claim: ZnF2 is the critical ZnF domain for SALL4 degradation.
source: However, the strength of the interaction with ZnF4 is unlikely to be sufficient for degradation in cells, and moreover, the rank order of Pom >Thal >> Len in binding observed with ZnF2 is in accordance with the cellular potency in degradation of SALL4, suggesting that ZnF2 is the critical ZnF domain for SALL4 degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from binding and degradation data.

claim: Mutations to alanine (G416A) in SALL4ZnF2 rendered SALL4ZnF2 resistant to IMiD-dependent binding to CRBN.
source: We confirmed the specificity of the SALL4ZnF2 interaction by introducing a point mutation to glycine 416 (G416), the residue critical for IMiD-dependent binding to CRBN (Petzold et al., 2016). Mutations to alanine (G416A) rendered SALL4ZnF2 resistant to IMiD-dependent binding to CRBN (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by TR-FRET binding data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Mutating glutamine 595 (Q595) in SALL4ZnF4 impaired IMiD-dependent binding.
source: Mutating glutamine 595 (Q595) in SALL4ZnF4, another residue previously shown to be critical for IMiD-dependent CRBN binding in the ZnF domains of IKZF1/3, impaired IMiD-dependent binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), confirming the specificity of the interaction despite the weak binding affinity.
evidence: This is supported by TR-FRET binding data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: G416N mutation in ZnF2, but not S388N mutation in ZnF1, fully abrogated IMiD-dependent binding of SALL4ZnF1-2 to CRBN.
source: We introduced the G416N mutation in ZnF2 or a S388N mutation in ZnF1 into the SALL4ZnF1-2 construct (S388 is the ZnF1 sequence equivalent of ZnF2 G416; ZnF1-2: C-x-x-C-S/G) and performed CRBN binding assays. G416N, but not S388N, fully abrogated IMiD-dependent binding of SALL4ZnF1-2 to CRBN (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–I), confirming the strict dependence on the ZnF2 interaction with CRBN.
evidence: This is supported by TR-FRET binding data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–I.

claim: Wild-type Flag-SALL4 was readily degraded by thalidomide treatment when expressed in Kelly cells.
source: To test whether the second zinc finger of SALL4 is critical for IMiD-induced degradation in cells, we introduced G416A and G416N mutations into Flag-tagged full-length SALL4. When expressed in Kelly cells, the parental wild-type Flag-SALL4 was readily degraded by thalidomide treatment (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Flag-tagged SALL4 with G600A or G600N mutations in ZnF4 were readily degraded with thalidomide treatment.
source: Similarly, Flag-tagged SALL4 with G600A or G600N mutations in ZnF4 were also shown to be readily degraded with thalidomide treatment, suggesting that SALL4ZnF4 is dispensable for binding and subsequent degradation (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: SALL4ZnF4 is dispensable for binding and subsequent degradation.
source: Similarly, Flag-tagged SALL4 with G600A or G600N mutations in ZnF4 were also shown to be readily degraded with thalidomide treatment, suggesting that SALL4ZnF4 is dispensable for binding and subsequent degradation (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is inferred from the degradation data showing that ZnF4 mutations do not prevent degradation.

claim: The two conservative mutations in ZnF2 (G416A or G416N) rendered SALL4 stable under thalidomide treatment conditions.
source: Finally, the two conservative mutations in ZnF2 (G416A or G416N), both known to specifically disrupt binding to CRBN while maintaining the overall zinc finger fold (Petzold et al., 2016), rendered SALL4 stable under these treatment conditions, demonstrating that SALL4ZnF2 is necessary for CRL4CRBN-mediated degradation of SALL4 in cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: SALL4ZnF2 is necessary for CRL4CRBN-mediated degradation of SALL4 in cells.
source: Finally, the two conservative mutations in ZnF2 (G416A or G416N), both known to specifically disrupt binding to CRBN while maintaining the overall zinc finger fold (Petzold et al., 2016), rendered SALL4 stable under these treatment conditions, demonstrating that SALL4ZnF2 is necessary for CRL4CRBN-mediated degradation of SALL4 in cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing that ZnF2 mutations prevent degradation.

claim: SALL4ZnF1-2 is ubiquitinated by CRL4CRBN in an IMiD-dependent fashion in vitro.
source: In vitro ubiquitination assays further confirm that SALL4ZnF1-2 is ubiquitinated by CRL4CRBN in an IMiD-dependent fashion (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: SALL4 is a bona fide IMiD-dependent target of CRL4CRBN.
source: Together, our cellular and biochemical data establish SALL4 as a bona fide IMiD-dependent target of CRL4CRBN, and demonstrate that the second zinc finger is necessary for IMiD-dependent degradation, while the tandem array of ZnF1-2 further strengthens the interaction in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence including binding, degradation, and ubiquitination assays.

claim: The second zinc finger is necessary for IMiD-dependent degradation of SALL4.
source: Together, our cellular and biochemical data establish SALL4 as a bona fide IMiD-dependent target of CRL4CRBN, and demonstrate that the second zinc finger is necessary for IMiD-dependent degradation, while the tandem array of ZnF1-2 further strengthens the interaction in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and degradation data.

claim: The tandem array of ZnF1-2 further strengthens the interaction with CRBN in vitro.
source: Together, our cellular and biochemical data establish SALL4 as a bona fide IMiD-dependent target of CRL4CRBN, and demonstrate that the second zinc finger is necessary for IMiD-dependent degradation, while the tandem array of ZnF1-2 further strengthens the interaction in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by binding affinity data comparing single and tandem ZnF constructs.

claim: Mouse Crbn harbors a critical polymorphism that prevents IMiD-dependent degradation of ZnF substrates and CSNK1A1.
source: Mouse Crbn harbors a critical polymorphism (Figure 4A,B and Figure 5) that prevents IMiD-dependent degradation of ZnF substrates and CSNK1A1 (Krönke et al., 2015), which could explain the absence of a SALL4-dependent phenotype in mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and sequence analysis shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 5.

claim: Mice and rats harbor an isoleucine at CRBN position 388.
source: Mice and rats (both insensitive to thalidomide embryopathies) harbor an isoleucine at CRBN position 388 (residue 388 refers to the human CRBN sequence).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Sensitive primates have a valine in position 388 of CRBN that is necessary for CRL4CRBN to bind, ubiquitinate, and subsequently degrade ZnF substrates.
source: In contrast, sensitive primates have a valine in position 388 that is necessary for CRL4CRBN to bind, ubiquitinate, and subsequently degrade ZnF substrates (Figure 4A,B and Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and binding data shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 5A.

claim: Treatment of mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC) with increasing concentrations of thalidomide or pomalidomide does not promote degradation of mmSALL4.
source: Consistent with this concept, treatment of mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC) with increasing concentrations of thalidomide or pomalidomide does not promote degradation of mmSALL4 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Introducing a V388I mutation into hsCRBN renders the protein less effective to bind to SALL4 in vitro.
source: Consistent with this concept, treatment of mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC) with increasing concentrations of thalidomide or pomalidomide does not promote degradation of mmSALL4 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and introducing a V388I mutation into hsCRBN renders the protein less effective to bind to SALL4 in vitro (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by TR-FRET binding data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Expression of hsCRBN in mouse cells sensitizes cells to degradation of IMiD targets such as mmIKZF1/3, mmCSNK1A1, mmZFP91, or mmGZF1.
source: Expression of hsCRBN in mouse cells, while sensitizing cells to degradation of IMiD targets such as mmIKZF1/3, mmCSNK1A1 (Krönke et al., 2015), mmZFP91, or mmGZF1 (Figure 4D,E), does not result in degradation of mmSALL4 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: Expression of hsCRBN in mouse cells does not result in degradation of mmSALL4.
source: Expression of hsCRBN in mouse cells, while sensitizing cells to degradation of IMiD targets such as mmIKZF1/3, mmCSNK1A1 (Krönke et al., 2015), mmZFP91, or mmGZF1 (Figure 4D,E), does not result in degradation of mmSALL4 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Ectopically expressed hsSALL4 is readily degraded upon IMiD treatment in Kelly cells.
source: To test whether a fully human CRBN in a human cell background would be sufficient to induce SALL4 degradation, we introduced hsSALL4, or mmSALL4 into human cells (Kelly cells) and found that while ectopically expressed hsSALL4 is readily degraded upon IMiD treatment, mmSALL4 is unaffected even at arbitrarily high doses of IMiDs (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: mmSALL4 is unaffected by IMiD treatment even at arbitrarily high doses when expressed in Kelly cells.
source: To test whether a fully human CRBN in a human cell background would be sufficient to induce SALL4 degradation, we introduced hsSALL4, or mmSALL4 into human cells (Kelly cells) and found that while ectopically expressed hsSALL4 is readily degraded upon IMiD treatment, mmSALL4 is unaffected even at arbitrarily high doses of IMiDs (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Mice and zebrafish have critical mutations in the ZnF2 domain of SALL4 which abrogate binding to hsCRBN in vitro.
source: Sequence analysis reveals that mice and zebrafish have critical mutations in the ZnF2 domain of SALL4 (Figure 5B), which abrogate binding to hsCRBN in vitro (Figure 4H)
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5B and TR-FRET binding data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: mmSALL4 and drSALL4 are insensitive to IMiD-mediated degradation in cells.
source: Sequence analysis reveals that mice and zebrafish have critical mutations in the ZnF2 domain of SALL4 (Figure 5B), which abrogate binding to hsCRBN in vitro (Figure 4H), and render mmSALL4 and drSALL4 insensitive to IMiD-mediated degradation in cells (Figure 4G,I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4G,I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mice harboring a homozygous CRBN I391V knock-in allele exhibit degradation of mmIKZF1/3, mmZFP91, and mmCSNK1A1.
source: In line with these findings, mice harboring a homozygous CRBN I391V knock-in allele, despite exhibiting degradation of mmIKZF1/3, mmZFP91, and mmCSNK1A1 Fink et al., 2018, show increased miscarriage upon IMiD treatment compared with control mice; however, they do not exhibit IMiD-induced embryopathies resembling the human phenotype Fink et al., 2018 .
evidence: This is supported by citation to a companion study.

claim: Mice harboring a homozygous CRBN I391V knock-in allele show increased miscarriage upon IMiD treatment compared with control mice.
source: In line with these findings, mice harboring a homozygous CRBN I391V knock-in allele, despite exhibiting degradation of mmIKZF1/3, mmZFP91, and mmCSNK1A1 Fink et al., 2018, show increased miscarriage upon IMiD treatment compared with control mice; however, they do not exhibit IMiD-induced embryopathies resembling the human phenotype Fink et al., 2018 .
evidence: This is supported by citation to a companion study.

claim: Mice harboring a homozygous CRBN I391V knock-in allele do not exhibit IMiD-induced embryopathies resembling the human phenotype.
source: In line with these findings, mice harboring a homozygous CRBN I391V knock-in allele, despite exhibiting degradation of mmIKZF1/3, mmZFP91, and mmCSNK1A1 Fink et al., 2018, show increased miscarriage upon IMiD treatment compared with control mice; however, they do not exhibit IMiD-induced embryopathies resembling the human phenotype Fink et al., 2018 .
evidence: This is supported by citation to a companion study.

claim: Through five amino acid substitutions required to 'humanize' the mmSALL4 ZnF2 domain, thalidomide-mediated mouse SALL4 degradation was induced in a human cell line.
source: We next sought to test whether exchange of the mmSALL4 ZnF2 domain for the hsSALL4 ZnF2 domain would be sufficient to enable mmSALL4 degradation in a human cell line (Kelly cells). Strikingly, through the five amino acid substitutions required to 'humanize' the mmSALL4 ZnF2 domain, we were able to induce thalidomide-mediated mouse SALL4 degradation in a human cell line (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: SALL4 degradation depends on both the sequence of SALL4 (zinc finger 2 differs between human and rodents), and the sequence of CRBN.
source: The observation that SALL4 degradation depends on both the sequence of SALL4 (zinc finger 2 differs between human and rodents), and the sequence of CRBN, supports a genetic cause for the species-specific effects, and highlights the complexities of modelling teratogenic adverse effects of IMiDs in murine and other animal models (Sakaki-Yumoto et al., 2006) (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on CRBN and SALL4 sequence differences and their effects on degradation.

claim: The only non-human primate known to be insensitive to thalidomide-induced embryopathies, the greater bush baby, harbors an isoleucine in the critical CRBN V388 position.
source: Of note, the only non-human primate known to be insensitive to thalidomide-induced embryopathies, the greater bush baby, also harbors an isoleucine in the critical CRBN V388 position (Butler, 1977)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research and sequence analysis.

claim: All sensitive non-human primates and rabbits harbor the conserved valine at CRBN position 388.
source: Of note, the only non-human primate known to be insensitive to thalidomide-induced embryopathies, the greater bush baby, also harbors an isoleucine in the critical CRBN V388 position (Butler, 1977), while all sensitive non-human primates and rabbits harbor the conserved valine (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Species can be rendered resistant to thalidomide by mutations in CRBN, SALL4, or both.
source: We thus show that species can be rendered resistant by mutations in CRBN, SALL4, or both, and hence our data suggest that thalidomide embryopathy is primarily a human disease (with some non-human primates, and rabbits more closely resembling the phenotypes), and thus explain the historic observation that modelling thalidomide embryopathies in animals is challenging.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on species-specific sequences and degradation patterns.

claim: Thalidomide embryopathy is primarily a human disease (with some non-human primates, and rabbits more closely resembling the phenotypes).
source: We thus show that species can be rendered resistant by mutations in CRBN, SALL4, or both, and hence our data suggest that thalidomide embryopathy is primarily a human disease (with some non-human primates, and rabbits more closely resembling the phenotypes), and thus explain the historic observation that modelling thalidomide embryopathies in animals is challenging.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the species-specific data.

claim: Zebrafish and chicken both contain an Ile in the V388 position of CRBN.
source: We note that zebrafish and chicken both contain an Ile in the V388 position; however, these were reported to exhibit defects to limb/fin formation upon exposure to thalidomide or knock-down of Crbn (Eichner et al., 2016; Ito et al., 2010), partially resembling thalidomide-induced defects.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and citation to prior research.

claim: Zebrafish and chicken were reported to exhibit defects to limb/fin formation upon exposure to thalidomide or knock-down of Crbn.
source: We note that zebrafish and chicken both contain an Ile in the V388 position; however, these were reported to exhibit defects to limb/fin formation upon exposure to thalidomide or knock-down of Crbn (Eichner et al., 2016; Ito et al., 2010), partially resembling thalidomide-induced defects.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Crbn knock-out mice have been reported to exhibit normal morphology.
source: These findings are in contrast with the observations in higher eukaryotes, as Crbn knock-out mice have been reported to exhibit normal morphology (Lee et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Children harboring a homozygous C391R mutation in CRBN were born without characteristic birth defects but exhibited severe neurological defects.
source: These findings are in contrast with the observations in higher eukaryotes, as Crbn knock-out mice have been reported to exhibit normal morphology (Lee et al., 2013), and children harboring a homozygous C391R mutation in CRBN (C391 is a structural cysteine coordinating the zinc in the thalidomide-binding domain of CRBN and we failed to produce any protein from a C391R cDNA), a loss of function mutation, were born without characteristic birth defects but exhibited severe neurological defects (Sheereen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: The plasma concentration of thalidomide in humans is unlikely to exceed 10 µM.
source: The plasma concentration of thalidomide in humans is, however, unlikely to exceed 10 µM (Bai et al., 2013; Dahut et al., 2009), a concentration that results in effective degradation of SALL4, but is 40 times below the dose found to be teratogenic in chicken and zebrafish embryos.
evidence: This is supported by citations to pharmacokinetic studies.

claim: A concentration of 10 µM thalidomide results in effective degradation of SALL4.
source: The plasma concentration of thalidomide in humans is, however, unlikely to exceed 10 µM (Bai et al., 2013; Dahut et al., 2009), a concentration that results in effective degradation of SALL4, but is 40 times below the dose found to be teratogenic in chicken and zebrafish embryos.
evidence: This is based on the degradation data from this study and pharmacokinetic data from citations.

claim: The dose found to be teratogenic in chicken and zebrafish embryos is 400 µM.
source: The plasma concentration of thalidomide in humans is, however, unlikely to exceed 10 µM (Bai et al., 2013; Dahut et al., 2009), a concentration that results in effective degradation of SALL4, but is 40 times below the dose found to be teratogenic in chicken and zebrafish embryos.
evidence: This is calculated from the statement that 10 µM is 40 times below the teratogenic dose.

claim: IMiDs lead to degradation of multiple ZnF transcription factors.
source: In fact, we show that IMiDs lead to degradation of multiple ZnF transcription factors, a class of proteins known to evolve very rapidly (Schmitges et al., 2016), and it is likely that IMiDs will exhibit species-specific effects.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomics data from this study.

claim: ZnF transcription factors are a class of proteins known to evolve very rapidly.
source: In fact, we show that IMiDs lead to degradation of multiple ZnF transcription factors, a class of proteins known to evolve very rapidly (Schmitges et al., 2016), and it is likely that IMiDs will exhibit species-specific effects.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: IMiD-dependent ZnF targets such as SALL4, ZNF653, ZNF692, or ZBTB39 are highly divergent even in higher eukaryotes.
source: Sequence analysis shows that IMiD-dependent ZnF targets such as SALL4, ZNF653, ZNF692, or ZBTB39, as well as other known genetic causes of limb defects in ZnF transcription factors, such as ESCO2, are highly divergent even in higher eukaryotes (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Thalidomide, lenalidomide, and pomalidomide all induce degradation of SALL4.
source: We show that thalidomide, lenalidomide, and pomalidomide all induce degradation of SALL4, which has been causatively linked to the most characteristic and common birth defects of the limbs and inner organs by human genetics.
evidence: This is supported by the degradation data from this study.

claim: SALL4 has been causatively linked to the most characteristic and common birth defects of the limbs and inner organs by human genetics.
source: We show that thalidomide, lenalidomide, and pomalidomide all induce degradation of SALL4, which has been causatively linked to the most characteristic and common birth defects of the limbs and inner organs by human genetics.
evidence: This is based on human genetic studies cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: SALL4 is consistently degraded across all IMiDs.
source: While other targets of thalidomide, such as CSNK1A1 for lenalidomide or GZF1, ZBTB39 for pomalidomide, may contribute to the pleiotropic developmental conditions observed upon thalidomide exposure, SALL4 is consistently degraded across all IMiDs and human geneticists associate heterozygous loss of SALL4 with human developmental syndromes that largely phenocopy thalidomide syndrome.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomics data from this study.

claim: Human geneticists associate heterozygous loss of SALL4 with human developmental syndromes that largely phenocopy thalidomide syndrome.
source: While other targets of thalidomide, such as CSNK1A1 for lenalidomide or GZF1, ZBTB39 for pomalidomide, may contribute to the pleiotropic developmental conditions observed upon thalidomide exposure, SALL4 is consistently degraded across all IMiDs and human geneticists associate heterozygous loss of SALL4 with human developmental syndromes that largely phenocopy thalidomide syndrome.
evidence: This is based on human genetic studies cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: IKZF1/3 have been shown to be non-causative for birth defects.
source: Moreover, from the targets degraded across IMiDs, IKZF1/3 have been shown to be non-causative for birth defects
evidence: This is based on prior knowledge or studies.

claim: RNF166 is a ubiquitin ligase involved in autophagy.
source: Moreover, from the targets degraded across IMiDs, IKZF1/3 have been shown to be non-causative for birth defects, RNF166 is a ubiquitin ligase involved in autophagy (Heath et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: ZNF692 knock-out mice do not exhibit a teratogenic phenotype.
source: Moreover, from the targets degraded across IMiDs, IKZF1/3 have been shown to be non-causative for birth defects, RNF166 is a ubiquitin ligase involved in autophagy (Heath et al., 2016), and ZNF692 knock-out mice do not exhibit a teratogenic phenotype (International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to mouse phenotyping data.

claim: The polypharmacology of IMiDs, together with the size and rapid evolution of the C2H2 family of zinc finger transcription factors, help to explain the pleiotropic effects of IMiDs.
source: The polypharmacology of IMiDs (most notably pomalidomide), together with the size and rapid evolution of the C2H2 family of zinc finger transcription factors (Figure 5D), which results in most C2H2 zinc finger transcription factors being highly species-specific (Najafabadi et al., 2015; Schmitges et al., 2016), help to explain the pleiotropic effects of IMiDs, which still remain largely understudied.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and cited literature.

claim: Most C2H2 zinc finger transcription factors are highly species-specific.
source: The polypharmacology of IMiDs (most notably pomalidomide), together with the size and rapid evolution of the C2H2 family of zinc finger transcription factors (Figure 5D), which results in most C2H2 zinc finger transcription factors being highly species-specific (Najafabadi et al., 2015; Schmitges et al., 2016), help to explain the pleiotropic effects of IMiDs, which still remain largely understudied.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The clinical features of IMiD efficacy as well as adverse effects are likely a result of induced degradation of multiple C2H2 zinc finger transcription factors.
source: Thalidomide embryopathies thus represent a case in which animal studies fall short, and it is likely that the clinical features of IMiD efficacy as well as adverse effects, are a result of induced degradation of multiple C2H2 zinc finger transcription factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing multiple ZnF targets.

claim: Mutations in GZF1 have been associated with joint laxity and short stature.
source: For example, we see some degree of degradation for GZF1, another C2H2 transcription factor, while GZF1 is unlikely to cause the defining birth defects of thalidomide, mutations in GZF1 have been associated with joint laxity and short stature, which are both also found in thalidomide-affected children (Patel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to genetic literature.

claim: CRBN expression levels influence the efficacy of IMiDs in inducing protein degradation.
source: We also note that CRBN expression levels influence the efficacy of IMiDs in inducing protein degradation, and it is conceivable that these contribute to a certain degree of tissue selectivity of IMiD effects, which for example, could increase the therapeutic index in MM as hematopoietic lineages tend to have high levels of CRBN.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of dose-response relationships and expression levels.

claim: Hematopoietic lineages tend to have high levels of CRBN.
source: We also note that CRBN expression levels influence the efficacy of IMiDs in inducing protein degradation, and it is conceivable that these contribute to a certain degree of tissue selectivity of IMiD effects, which for example, could increase the therapeutic index in MM as hematopoietic lineages tend to have high levels of CRBN.
evidence: This is based on expression data or prior knowledge.

claim: Thalidomide teratogenicity affected more than 10,000 individuals.
source: Thalidomide teratogenicity was a severe and widespread public health tragedy, affecting more than 10,000 individuals, and the aftermath has shaped many of the current drug regulatory procedures.
evidence: This is a historical fact.

claim: Thalidomide and its derivatives induce degradation of SALL4, providing a direct link to genetic disorders of SALL4 deficiency, which phenocopy many of the teratogenic effects of thalidomide.
source: Our findings that thalidomide and its derivatives induce degradation of SALL4, provide a direct link to genetic disorders of SALL4 deficiency, which phenocopy many of the teratogenic effects of thalidomide.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on SALL4 degradation and genetic phenotypes.

claim: Degradation of SALL4 is likely to contribute to birth defects caused by thalidomide.
source: While other effects of thalidomide, such as anti-angiogenic properties may contribute to birth defects, degradation of SALL4 is likely to contribute to birth defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and phenotypic overlap.

claim: These findings can inform the development of new compounds that induce CRBN-dependent degradation of disease-relevant proteins but avoid degradation of developmental transcription factors such as SALL4.
source: These findings can inform the development of new compounds that induce CRBN-dependent degradation of disease-relevant proteins but avoid degradation of developmental transcription factors such as SALL4, and thus have the potential for therapeutic efficacy without the risk of teratogenicity, a defining feature of this class of drugs.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement based on the findings.

claim: IMiD-based PROTACs and novel IMiD derivatives such as CC-220 can be effective inducers of ZnF targets including SALL4 degradation.
source: This is further relevant to the development of thalidomide-derived bifunctional small molecule degraders (commonly referred to as PROTACs) (Raina and Crews, 2017), as we show that IMiD-based PROTACs (and novel IMiD derivatives such as CC-220) can be effective inducers of ZnF targets including SALL4 degradation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The surprising expansion in substrate repertoire for pomalidomide suggests that IMiDs exhibit a large degree of polypharmacology contributing to both efficacy and adverse effects.
source: Lastly, the surprising expansion in substrate repertoire for pomalidomide, suggests that IMiDs exhibit a large degree of polypharmacology contributing to both efficacy and adverse effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the proteomics data showing many pomalidomide-specific targets.

claim: IMiDs and related compounds are likely to exhibit species-specific effects by virtue of their mode of action.
source: Transcription factors, and specifically C2H2 zinc fingers are highly divergent between species, and hence IMiDs and related compounds are likely to exhibit species-specific effects by virtue of their mode of action.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the species-specific data and the divergence of ZnF proteins.

claim: The discovery that IMiDs target an unanticipated large set of C2H2 zinc finger proteins with significant differences among thalidomide, lenalidomide, pomalidomide, and CC-220, suggests that this chemical scaffold holds the potential to target one of the largest families of human transcription factors.
source: In turn, the discovery that IMiDs target an unanticipated large set of C2H2 zinc finger proteins with significant differences among thalidomide, lenalidomide, pomalidomide, and CC-220, suggests that this chemical scaffold holds the potential to target one of the largest families of human transcription factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the proteomics data showing multiple ZnF targets.
